title: Self-Organizing Tissue, Measured Against Fetal Cortex

scenes.tts: In 2013, a laboratory in Vienna grew brain-like tissue in a dish. It came from the skin cells of a person with severe microcephaly, a brain far smaller than normal. The zones of dividing cortical progenitors in that tissue were smaller than in tissue from control cells. Could skin cells become a model of early cortex? And how far can that model be trusted?
scenes.visual: Skin cell, question mark, then folded tissue; two tissues compare progenitor zones, patient smaller; a question closes the scene.

scenes.tts: First, the skin cell has to return to an embryonic state. Four transcription factors can do that. Transcription factors are proteins that bind D N A and turn genes on or off. In human skin cells, the four factors made induced pluripotent stem cells. Pluripotent means able to give rise to every cell type of the body. A line made from a patient carries the patient's whole genome, mutation included.
scenes.visual: Skin cell, four factor chips, arrow to a pluripotent cell that carries the patient's genome.

scenes.tts: Next, the cells are gathered into a ball and steered toward neural tissue. The ball is embedded in a droplet of gel. Then it goes into a spinning flask, where moving medium improves the supply of oxygen and nutrients. The cells arrange themselves. That is self-organization, and it is the idea behind every organoid.
scenes.visual: Scattered cells gather into a ball, gel ring, spinning flask arrows, then the cells rearrange around a cavity.

scenes.tts: Inside, regions form that look like early cortex. Radial glia surround a fluid-filled cavity. Their nuclei move toward the cavity and away again as the cells divide. Beyond them sit intermediate progenitors, and further out, early neurons. A comparison with developing human cortex found the same broad classes of cells.
scenes.visual: Cross-section enlarges: radial glia around a cavity with nuclei moving, intermediate progenitors, early neurons, broad classes match.

scenes.tts: The match has limits. Standard organoids have no blood vessels, so the center of a large one often dies. Finer cell subtypes blur: organoid cells often resemble several subtypes in developing cortex about equally. Stress genes run higher in organoid cells, and they fell after transplant into mouse cortex, which suggests the culture environment contributes. And most organoids model early and mid-fetal stages, not a mature brain.
scenes.visual: Four panels: no vessels and a dying center, blurred subtypes, stress bars falling after transplant, a timeline of fetal stages.

scenes.tts: One patient's organoids could be smaller because of the gene, the rest of that person's genes, a quirk of one cell line, or a bad batch. So use several clones from the patient and several controls from different people, grown side by side, more than once. Then put the gene back into patient tissue, or remove it from a control, and see whether the result follows. Resemblance has to be measured, and a mutation is blamed only after the controls.
scenes.visual: Four candidate causes, a grid of lines by batch, gene put back, closing rule.
